claims.text: FeCoCrMnNi is a five-element random high-entropy alloy.
The cited FeCoCrMnNi example is equiatomic.
FeCoCrMnNi exhibits local force-constant fluctuations of approximately 20%.
FeCoCrMnNi has stronger acoustic-phonon attenuation than simple elements.
Force-constant fluctuations arising from atomic disorder scatter phonons in FeCoCrMnNi.
High-entropy-alloy lattice distortion can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low lattice thermal conductivity.
Increasing temperature from 300 to 700 K can decrease lattice thermal conductivity through increased phonon scattering in the cited low-conductivity high-entropy system.

A machine-learning framework integrating DFT-derived local force constants and phonon dispersions with experimental phonon lifetimes will predict low lattice thermal conductivity more accurately than averaged lattice-dynamics models.
Explicitly representing local vibrational anomalies will allow the model to correlate atomic disorder with enhanced phonon scattering.
Modeling local vibrational anomalies will improve predictions of phonon lifetimes.
Improved phonon-lifetime predictions will produce more precise predictions of overall lattice thermal conductivity.
Conventional averaged lattice-dynamics and simple-scattering models inadequately represent local force-constant fluctuations and vibrational heterogeneity.
The machine-learning approach will reduce lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20–30% relative to conventional models.
The machine-learning approach will reliably identify high-entropy alloys with lattice thermal conductivity below 2 W m−1 K−1.
The approach is applicable primarily to near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys at 300–700 K when their disorder lies within the training-data range.
The approach may not apply to alloys with extreme compositional deviations.
Substantial phase transitions may invalidate the approach by altering local disorder.
The hypothesis is falsified if the model fails to lower prediction error by at least 20–30% relative to conventional averaged models under the specified test conditions.
